newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada diamond mine expects sales plan in six months.
newsitem.headline: Canada diamond mine expects sales plan in six months.

text.p: The developers of a diamond mine in Canada's Arctic expect to decide within six months on a strategy that may include selling the stones outside of the De Beers cartel, which controls the world's diamond market.

The Lac de Gras mine is being built by Australia's Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd., which has a 51 percent stake, in a joint venture with Canada's Dia Met Minerals Ltd. . Production is scheduled to begin in late 1998.
"Within six months, we will have a marketing program," Dia Met President Jim Eccott said in an interview on Monday. "By June, we hope to decide what channels we will sell through."
Those could entail selling "independently or through the CSO (De Beers' Central Selling Organization)...or a combination" of the methods, he said.
"Naturally De Beers is very anxious for us to market through them, but there are a lot of factors to be looked at," he said, declining to elaborate.

Speculation in the diamond world that the Canadian mine could bypass the CSO has fanned talk that De Beers' grip on the market may be loosening.

De Beers' control has also been threatened by its failure so far to renew a gem export deal with Russia, a major producer. The Argyle diamond mine in Australia, the world's largest owned by RTZ Corp. - CRA Ltd, last year announced it was pulling out of the CSO.

Eccott said that Dia Met, which has 29 percent of the Lac de Gras project, was expected to sell its share of the diamonds together with BHP. Under their agreement, Dia Met has the right to sell its share of the production independently once it pays BHP back for its share of the mine production costs, expected to be in about three years.
But Eccott said Dia Met has no desire to circumvent BHP. "There's no question...we're all working together," he said. "We are not going to take the diamonds and start selling them around the world."

Aber Resources Ltd., a Vancouver company that is developing a diamond project near the Lac de Gras mine site with the Kennecott unit of RTZ, said on Monday it had also met with De Beers but was investigating independent sales too.

While no decision had been made, its mine could go into production around the turn of the century. Aber had the right to market its 40 percent of the diamonds on its own, spokesman Frank Bradley said.

Canada could eventually become one of the world's top five diamond producers based on output from the Lac de Gras mine and others in the same area, Burne estimated. Lac de Gras is projected to produce three to five million carats of diamonds a year over 25 years with a high proportion of gems, the most profitable segment off the market.
